title: Christ, the near angels and contextual comparison
ar: ومنها قوله تعالي لن يستنكف المسيح ان يكون عبدا لله ولا الملاءكة المقربون اي لا يترفع عيسي في العبودية ولا من هو ارفع منه درجة كقولك لن يستنكف من هذا الامر الوزير ولا السلطان ولو عكست احلت بشهادة علماء البيان والبصراء باساليب الكلام وعليه قوله تعالي ولن ترضي عنك اليهود ولا النصاري اي مع انهم اقرب مودة لاهل الاسلام ولهذا خص الملاءكة بالمقربين منهم لكونهم افضل والجواب ان الكلام سبق لرد مقالة النصاري وغيرهم في المسيح وادعاءهم فيه مع النبوة البنوة بل الالوهية والترفع عن العبودية لكونه روح الله ولد بلا اب ولكونه يبرء الاكمه والابرص والمعني لا يترفع عيسي عن العبودية ولا من هو فوقه في هذا المعني وهم الملاءكة الذين لا اب لهم ولا ام ويقدرون علي مالا يقدر عليه عيسي عليه السلام ولا دلالة علي الافضلية بمعني كثرة الثواب وساءر الكمالات الا يري ان فيما ذكرت من المثال لم يقصد الزيادة والرفعة في الفضل والشرف والكمال بل فيما هو مظنة الاستنكاف والرضا كالغلبة والاستكبار والاستعلاء في السلطان وقرب المودة في النصاري

en: “Christ will not disdain being God's servant, nor will the angels brought near” is read as an ascending comparison: neither the minister nor even the sovereign would refuse an act, so the angels must outrank Jesus. **Reply:** The text replies to Christian claims that Christ's fatherless birth, miracles and status as God's spirit lift him above servanthood. Angels are “above him” **in the features imagined to give an excuse for refusing to serve**: they have neither father nor mother and can perform acts beyond those of Jesus. The comparison thus concerns a supposed reason for disdain, not an absolute ranking in reward and all other perfections. Likewise, the comparison “Neither Jews nor Christians will be pleased with you” is ordered according to a contextual relation (comparative closeness of affection), not absolute value.

en: **Investigation eight.** A *walī* (friend of God, saint) is someone who knows God and His attributes, perseveres in acts of obedience, avoids disobedience, and turns away from immersion in sensual pleasures and desires. His *karāma* is the appearance, on his behalf, of something that contravenes ordinary custom **without accompanying a claim to prophethood**. That last qualification distinguishes *karāma* from *muʿjiza*, a miracle confirming a prophetic claim. Its association with right belief, righteous action and adherence to a prophet distinguishes it from *istidrāj*, the extraordinary occurrence that may lead the wicked further astray, and from signs that expose false claimants. Thus a report concerning Musaylima alleges that he prayed for a one-eyed person's damaged eye to be made sound, whereupon the healthy eye became blind instead; this is called *ihāna*, humiliation. Extraordinary assistance shown to ordinary Muslims to rescue them from affliction is called *maʿūna*. Accordingly, four forms of extraordinary occurrence are distinguished: *muʿjiza*, *karāma*, *maʿūna* and *ihāna*.

en: Most Muslims, the author reports, accept the possibility of saintly wonders; many Muʿtazilites deny them. According to Imām al-Ḥaramayn, Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī leans toward the latter position. Among those allowing wonders, some disallow their occurrence through the saint's purpose and choice; others exclude wonders that vindicate an explicit claim to sanctity, since making such a claim or expecting extraordinary occurrences could compromise sainthood; yet others exclude exactly the types of events that served as prophetic miracles, such as parting a sea, changing a staff into a serpent, or reviving the dead. These proposed distinctions purport to protect the difference between saints and prophets.

ar: وللمخالف وجوه الاول وهو العمدة انه لو ظهرت الخوارق من الولي لالتبس النبي بغيره اذ الفارق هو المعجزة ورد بما مر من الفرق بين المعجزة والكرامة

title: Fifth objection: unseen knowledge, scope of negation and revelation
ar: الخامس وهو في الاخبار عن المغيبات قوله تعالي عالم الغيب فلا يظهر علي غيبه احدا الا من ارتضي من رسول خص الرسل من بين المرتضين بالاطلاع علي الغيب فلا يطلع غيرهم وان كانوا اولياء مرتضين فما يشاهد من الكهنة القاء الجن والشياطين ومن اصحاب التعبير والنجوم ظنون واستدلالات ربما تقع وربما لا تقع ليس من اطلاع الله تعالي في شء والجواب ان الغيب ههنا ليس للعموم بل مطلق او معين هو وقت وقوع القيمة بقرينة السياق ولا يبعد ان يطلع عليه بعض الرسل من الملاءكة او البشر فيصح الاستثناء وان جعل منقطعا فلا خفاء بل لا امتناع حينءذ في جعل الغيب للعموم لكون اسم الجنس المضاف بمنزلة المعرف باللام سيما وقد كان في الاصل مصدرا ويكون الكلام لسلب العموم اي لا يطلع علي كل غيبه احد او هو لا ينافي اطلاع البعض علي البعض وكذا لا اشكال ان خص الاطلاع بطريق الوحي وبالجملة فالاستدلال مبني علي ان الكلام لعموم السلب اي لا يطلع علي شء من غيبه احدا من الافراد نوعا من الاطلاع وذلك ليس بلازم

en:
**Fifth argument, specifically about hidden knowledge:** “Knower of the unseen; He does not disclose His unseen to anyone except a messenger whom He approves” appears to restrict access to the unseen to chosen messengers. Accordingly, saints—even favoured saints—could have no such disclosure; what diviners obtain from jinn or devils is one thing, and what interpreters of dreams or astrologers infer conjecturally is another, but none is a disclosure of God's unseen. **Reply:** “The unseen” need not encompass everything hidden. It may be unrestricted in expression but not universally quantified, or may refer to a particular concealed fact, such as the date of the Resurrection suggested by the context. God might disclose that event to some messengers, whether angelic or human, and the exception is then meaningful. Even if the exception is taken as *disconnected* (*munqaṭiʿ*), the name “unseen” may be generic without making the clause exclude every instance of disclosure. “He does not disclose His unseen to anyone” may deny that **anyone knows the whole of His unseen**, not that somebody can know **some** of it. The objection likewise dissolves if the particular disclosure reserved to messengers is disclosure through revelation (*waḥy*). In sum, the argument only succeeds on a strict reading of universal negation: that no individual other than a messenger can receive any form of disclosure of even one hidden matter. That reading is not forced by the wording.

**Logical point:** the final inference equivocates between a universal negative—*no one is ever apprised of any unseen matter*—and denial of unrestricted knowledge—*no one is apprised of all God’s unseen matters*. The source explicitly names this contrast *ʿumūm al-salb* and *salb al-ʿumūm*.

title: The reported claims about prophetic and saintly rank
ar: قال خاتمة حكي عن بعض الكرامية ان الولي قد يبلغ درجة النبي بل اعلي وعن بعض الصوفية ان الولاية افضل من النبوة لانها تنبء عن القرب والكرامة كما هو شان خواص الملك والمقربين منه والنبوة عن الانباء والتبليغ كما هو حال من ارسله الملك الي الرعايا لتبليغ احكامه الا ان الولي لا يبلغ درجة النبي لان النبوة لا تكون بدون الولاية وعن اهل الاباحة والالحاد ان الولي اذا بلغ الغاية في المحبة وصفاء القلب وكمال الاخلاص سقط عنه الامر والنهي ولم يضره الذنب ولا يدخل النار بارتكاب الكبيرة والكل فاسد باجماع المسلمين

en: **Conclusion.** Some Karrāmiyya are reported as saying that a saint can reach the same rank as a prophet or higher. Some Sufis are reported as saying that *walāya* (friendship with God, saintship) is higher than *nubuwwa* (prophethood), because the former denotes nearness and distinction, like the king's intimates, whereas the latter denotes conveying information and instructions, like a king's envoy sent to subjects. Yet they add that **no saint can attain the rank of a prophet**, since prophethood is never without sainthood. The permissivists and antinomians (*ahl al-ibāḥa wa-l-ilḥād*) are reported to claim that the perfected saint, once he reaches the limit of love, purity of heart and sincerity, is no longer subject to command and prohibition, and that his sins cannot harm him or bring punishment even for grave wrongs. The author rejects all these positions as **unqualified doctrinal propositions** by the consensus of Muslims.

title: The prophet’s combined perfections and the two-sided mission
ar: والاول خاصة بان النبي مع ماله من شرف الولاية معصوم عن المعاصي مامون عن سوء العاقبة بحكم النصوص القاطعة مشرف بالوحي ومشاهدة الملك مبعوث لاصلاح حال العالم ونظام امر المعاش والمعاد الي غير ذلك من الكمالات والثاني بان النبوة تنبء عن البعثة والتبليغ من الحق الي الخلق ففيها ملاحظة للجانبين ويتضمن قرب الولاية وشرفها لا محالة فلا تقصر عن مرتبة ولاية غير الانبياء لانها لا تكون علي غاية الكمال لان علامة ذلك نيل مرتبة النبوة

title: A qualified mystical statement about enduring sainthood
ar: وفي كلام بعض العرفاء ان ما قيل الولاية افضل من النبوة لا يصح مطلقا وليس من الادب اطلاق القول به بل لا بد من التقييد وهو ان ولاية النبي افضل من نبوته لان نبوة التشريع متعلقة بمصلحة الوقت والولاية لا تعلق لها بوقت دون وقت بل قام سلطانها الي قيام الساعة بخلاف النبوة فانها مختومة بمحمد صلي الله عليه وسلم من حيث ظاهرها الذي هو الانباء وان كانت داءمة من حيث باطنها الذي هو الولاية اعني التصرف في الخلق بالحق فان الاولياء من امة محمد صلي الله عليه وسلم حملة تصرف ولايته بهم يتصرف في الخلق بالحق الي قيام الساعة ولهذا كانت علامتهم المتابعة اذ ليس الولي الا مظهر تصرف النبي

Outward prophethood was sealed by Muḥammad; its inward reality, the saintly governance of creatures through the Real (*al-taṣarruf fī-l-khalq bi-l-ḥaqq*), continues through saints of his community. title: Spiritual absorption, loss of responsibility and “rational madmen”
ar: نعم حكي عن بعض الاولياء انه استعفي الله عن التكاليف وساله الاعتاق عن ظواهر العبادات فاجابه الي ذلك بان سلبه العقل الذي هو مناط التكليف ومع ذلك كان من علو المرتبة علي ما كان وانت خبير بان العارف لا يسام من العبادة ولا يفتر في الطاعة ولا يسال الهبوط من اوج الكمال الي حضيض النقصان والنزول من معارج الملك الي منازل الحيوان بل ربما يحصل له كمال الانجذاب الي عالم القدس والاستغراق في ملاحظة جناب الحق بحيث يذهل عن هذا العالم ويخل بالتكاليف من غير تاثم بذلك لكونه في حكم غير المكلف كالناءم وذلك لعجزه عن مراعاة الامرين وملاحظة الجانبين فربما يسال دوام تلك الحالة وعدم العود الي عالم الظاهر وهذا الذهول هو الجنون الذي ربما يترجح علي بعض العقول والمتسمون به هم المسمون بمجانين العقلاء

en: A story is told of a saint who asked God to exempt him from the outward forms of worship and was answered by being deprived of the intellect on which responsibility (*taklīf*) depends, while still remaining at his former spiritual rank. The commentator objects that a true knower of God does not tire of worship, grow weary of obedience, or seek to descend from the summit of perfection to deficiency, from an angelic ascent to an animal level. Something different may occur: a person can become so perfectly attracted toward the holy world and absorbed in awareness of God that he is distracted from this world and neglects outward duties without sin, because he is like someone no longer responsible, just as a sleeper is, being incapable of attending simultaneously to both planes. Such a person might desire the continuation of this state and not to return to ordinary outward awareness. This *dhuhūl* (absorption or obliviousness) is the kind of “madness” which can surpass certain forms of ordinary reason; those so described are called the “rational madmen” (*majānīn al-ʿuqalāʾ*).

ar: وبهذا يظهر فضل الانبياء علي الاولياء فانهم مع ان استغراقهم اكمل وانجذابهم اشمل لا يخلون بادني طاعة ولا يذهلون من هذا الجانب ساعة لان قوتهم القدسية من الكمال بحيث لا يشغلها شاغل عن ذلك الجناب ولهذا ينعي عليهم ادني زلة عن منهج الصواب قال

ar: وعلي الوقوع وجوه منها قوله تعالي يعلمون الناس السحر وما انزل علي الملكين ببابل هاروت وماروت الي قوله فيتعلمون منهما ما يفرقون به بين المرء وزوجه وما هم بضارين به من احد الا باذن الله وفيه اشعار بانه ثابت حقيقة ليس مجرد اراءة وتمويه وبان المءثر والخالق هو الله وحده ومنها سورة الفلق فقد اتفق جمهور المسلمين علي انها نزلت فيما كانت من سحر لبيد بن اعصم اليهودي لرسول الله صلي الله عليه وسلم حتي مرض ثلاث ليال ومنها ما روي ان جارية سحرت عاءشة رضي الله تعالي عنها وانه سحر ابن عمر رضي الله تعالي عنه فتكوعت يده

title: Objection from universal magical power and protection of prophets
section: Investigation IX: siḥr and the evil eye
ar: فان قيل لو صح السحر لاضرت السحرة بجميع الانبياء والصالحين ولحصلوا لانفسهم الملك العظيم وكيف يصح ان يسحر النبي صلي الله عليه وسلم وقد قال الله تعالي والله يعصمك من الناس ولا يفلح الساحر حيث اتي وكان الكفرة يعيبون النبي صلي الله عليه وسلم بانه مسحور مع القطع بانهم كاذبون قلنا ليس الساحر يوجد في كل عصر وزمان وبكل قطر ومكان ولا ينفذ حكمه كل اوان ولا له يد في كل شان والنبي معصوم من ان يهلكه الناس او يوقع خللا في نبوته لا ان يوصل ضررا والما الي بدنه ومراد الكفار بكونه مسحورا انه مجنون ازيل عقله بالسحر حيث ترك دينهم

en: **Objection:** If magic were effective, magicians could harm all prophets and righteous people and win great kingdoms for themselves. title: The magicians of Moses and real effects through induced appearance
section: Investigation IX: siḥr and the evil eye
ar: فان قيل قوله تعالي في قصة موسي صلي الله تعالي عليه وسلم يخيل اليه من سحرهم انها تسعي يدل علي انه لا حقيقة للسحر وانما هو تخيل وتمويه قلنا يجوز ان يكون سحرهم هو ايقاع ذلك التخييل وقد تحقق ولو سلم فيكون اثره في تلك الصورة هو التحييل لا يدل علي انه لا حقيقة له اصلا

en: **Objection:** Moses perceived the magicians' ropes and staffs as moving although they did not; the Qurʾān thus says that magic is simply illusion. **Reply:** The real magical effect might be precisely **the production of that appearance in the perceiver**. Even supposing that their particular feat was deception, that establishes only the nature of this instance, not the unreality of all magic.

title: The evil eye, admiration and al-Jubbāʾī’s objection
section: Investigation IX: siḥr and the evil eye
ar: واما الاصابة بالعين وهو ان يكون لبعض النفوس خاصية انها اذا استحسنت شيءا لحقته الافة فثبوتها يكاد يجري مجري المشاهدات التي لا تفتقر الي حجة وقد قال النبي صلي الله عليه وسلم العين حق وقال العين تدخل الرجل القبر والجمل القدر وذهب كثير من المفسرين الي ان قوله تعالي وان يكاد الذين كفروا ليزلقونك بابصارهم الاية نزل في ذلك وقالوا ان كان العين في بني اسد وكان الرجل منهم يتجوع ثلاثة ايام فلا يمر به شء يقول فيه لم ار كاليوم الاعانة فالتمس الكفار من بعض من كانت له هذه الصفة ان يقول في رسول الله صلي الله عليه وسلم ذلك فعصمه الله واعترض الجباءي بان القوم ما كانوا ينظرون الي النبي صلي الله عليه وسلم نظراستحسان بل مقت وبغض والجواب انهم كانوا يستحسنون منه الفصاحة وكثيرا من الصفات وان كانوا يبغضونه من جهة الدين

section: Investigation IX: siḥr and the evil eye

en: Among those who accept magic and the evil eye there remain disagreements concerning protective recitations (*ruqā*), refuge formulas (*ʿuwadh*), hanging amulets (*tamāʾim*), blowing (*nafth*) and touching or wiping (*masḥ*). Reports and early precedents are cited on both sides; the author judges permission preferable and remarks that the issue properly belongs to jurisprudence rather than to the central principles of theology. He concludes that permission is the stronger view (*al-jawāz arjaḥ*), that the question more properly belongs to the legal disciplines, and closes with: **God knows** (*wa-li-llāhi ʿilm* in the electronic witness).

title: Resurrection: what “return” means, and the possibility of restoring an existent
en:
**Chapter two: The Resurrection (*al-maʿād*).** “Return” (*ʿawd*) is a verbal noun or a noun of place, and its literal meaning is that a thing comes back to what it formerly was. Here the intended return may be (a) existence after annihilation, (b) the gathering of bodily parts after their dispersal and the revival of the body after death, and (c) the restoration of departed souls to bodies. A merely spiritual resurrection, as held by certain philosophers, instead means the soul's return to its previous condition of separation from bodily involvement and use of instruments, or its purification from the darknesses to which its bodily condition exposed it.

**Investigation one: Can something nonexistent return numerically as itself?** Many inquiries in scholastic theology appear extraneous to religious beliefs, yet their role becomes clear when the principal aims are examined. They provide arguments or refute doubts concerning such doctrines. The return of the nonexistent, indivisible parts, void, annihilation of the world, the possibility of opening the celestial spheres, the independence of life from a specific organic arrangement, and the possible non-finitude of bodily powers are invoked in establishing bodily resurrection, grave punishment and everlasting life in Paradise or Hell, according to differing theological premises. The author postponed the problem of the **re-creation of a nonexistent** to this point because it bears especially on resurrection understood as **existence after complete annihilation**.

Most theologians accept that such restoration is possible; philosophers regard it as impossible. Among the Muʿtazila, those other than the Basran school permit the return of substances on the assumption that their essences remain established even in nonexistence: if the essence itself were to perish, its return would be impossible. They differ over accidents. Some reject the restoration of any accident, claiming that a returned accident would have to be restored as an attribute in another and thus entail the inherence of one attribute in another; some of the author's colleagues are also said to hold this. Most Muʿtazilites disallow the restoration of accidents that cannot persist, such as sounds and acts of willing, because they belong to particular instants. Among enduring accidents they distinguish those within a servant's power, which they say neither servant nor Lord can restore, from those not within a servant's power, which they allow God to restore.

**Initial argument for possibility, by persuasion:** In the absence of proof of impossibility or necessity, the default is to leave a matter within the field of possibility. The philosophers themselves say that any remarkable report reaching your ears should be allowed a place among the possible until a decisive demonstration excludes it. Whoever denies that the nonexistent can return must supply that proof.

**Argument by compelling analogy:** The renewed thing would be **the same as the original**, indeed numerically identical, for that is the very point in question. What is intrinsically possible cannot become intrinsically impossible solely because time has passed; time has no power to alter what belongs to a thing in virtue of itself. The objection that *second* existence is a narrower notion than existence as such, and that possibility of the wider does not entail possibility of the narrower, does not apply if the numerically same thing itself is at issue.

A related argument begins with the nonexistent possible thing's capacity to receive existence; intrinsic possibility is not reversed by a change of temporal location. If the first existence confers a greater readiness for existence—as recipients often acquire a habit through actualization—the second actualization would be **easier** for the recipient and nearer to it. This may be the correct sense of “He originates creation and then restores it, and that is easier for Him.” If existence confers no such heightened aptitude, it certainly does not remove the intrinsic potentiality that the thing had from the outset.

Yet the author judges it closer to the intended meaning of the verse that the restoration called “easier” is the reconstitution of surviving bodily parts and dispersed material into their former forms and combinations, as indicated by “Say: He will give them life who originated them the first time,” rather than the restoration of a **wholly nonexistent** thing. In the latter case there remains no recipient, much less any increased preparedness inhering in that recipient.

**Objection:** How could any act be “easier” for God when His power is eternal and all its objects stand equally in relation to it? **Reply:** An act may be easier because the agent's conditions of agency are improved or because the recipient's receptivity is enhanced. Only the second sense is involved here; relative to divine power itself, all things are alike.

**Further objection:** All that has been established is that the nonexistent is intrinsically able to exist later, which does not exclude a necessary concomitant preventing its later existence—for example, that there is then nothing to point to or predicate of. More importantly, the issue is not existence in general but the **return of precisely the same individual** for a second existence. **Reply:** If the nonexistent were prevented from existing by something necessarily belonging to it, it would already have been prevented from existing at the outset, just as though it were intrinsically impossible. Possibility of existence entails possibility of bringing into existence, especially for one and the same divine power. And “return” here designates the **condition of having returned**, that is, second existence of the same individual.

The philosophers themselves say that any remarkable report reaching your ears should be allowed a place among the possible until a decisive demonstration excludes it. Whoever denies that the nonexistent can return must supply that proof.

Argument by compelling analogy: The renewed thing would be the same as the original, indeed numerically identical, for that is the very point in question. What is intrinsically possible cannot become intrinsically impossible solely because time has passed; time has no power to alter what belongs to a thing in virtue of itself. The objection that second existence is a narrower notion than existence as such, and that possibility of the wider does not entail possibility of the narrower, does not apply if the numerically same thing itself is at issue.

A related argument begins with the nonexistent possible thing's capacity to receive existence; intrinsic possibility is not reversed by a change of temporal location. Reply: An act may be easier because the agent's conditions of agency are improved or because the recipient's receptivity is enhanced. Further objection: All that has been established is that the nonexistent is intrinsically able to exist later, which does not exclude a necessary concomitant preventing its later existence—for example, that there is then nothing to point to or predicate of. More importantly, the issue is not existence in general but the return of precisely the same individual for a second existence. Reply: If the nonexistent were prevented from existing by something necessarily belonging to it, it would already have been prevented from existing at the outset, just as though it were intrinsically impossible. Possibility of existence entails possibility of bringing into existence, especially for one and the same divine power. And “return” here designates the condition of having returned, that is, second existence of the same individual.

title: Four demonstrations against re-creation, with their replies
en:
**Those denying the restoration of the nonexistent** fall into different groups. Some take impossibility as self-evident: once a mind is free of imitation and partisanship, it cannot hesitate in judging that what exists for a second time is not numerically identical to what existed first. Al-Rāzī is quoted approving this claim in the *Mabāḥith al-mashriqiyya/al-Mabāḥith al-ʿāliya* tradition [exact title requires verification]: every mind returning to its healthy constitution, without partisan preference, testifies to the impossibility of restoring what is wholly nonexistent. **Reply:** The claim to self-evidence is denied. Numerous rational thinkers have accepted the opposite and argued for it; therefore its rejection is not a universal immediate judgement.

**First demonstration:** If the nonexistent were restored as itself, nonexistence would intervene between a thing **and itself**—an evident absurdity. **Reply:** The alleged absurdity disappears when the two times are distinguished: strictly, nonexistence intervenes between **the two times of the existence of the same individual**. Being prior at one time and posterior at another does not destroy numerical unity. There is no more intrinsic contradiction in nonexistence intervening between two existences than in existence intervening between earlier and later nonexistence. The author criticizes treating this argument, as the *Mawāqif* allegedly does, as a mere elucidation of an immediately evident principle: an argument's premise may be self-evident without its conclusion being so, and such a treatment misrepresents both the argument and the underlying problem.

**Second demonstration:** If the nonexistent returned with **all** its individuating features, its first time would have to return as well, since time is one such feature: being present **at this instant** differs from being present **at that instant**. If times themselves can be re-created, then the restored object is also newly originated **by virtue of its being restored**, for to originate is to exist at the first time; thus the same thing would be both first-originated and restored in the same respect and at the same time. Alternatively, the distinction between beginning and returning would vanish: the second occurrence would count as a return only because it counted as an initial occurrence. These results, or the contradictions implicit in them, are sometimes presented as three distinct objections.

**Reply:** Time is not accepted as one of the intrinsically individuating constituents. We know that the book before us today is **the very same book** that was present yesterday; someone denying this on the mere ground of changed time would be treated as a sophist. Different temporal relationships and aspects do not negate numerical identity in external reality. Even if the earlier time itself could be restored, existence in a first time would not necessarily make an occurrence “first-originated”: that would follow only if the time had not itself returned or had not previously occurred. More exactly, *first-originated* means what occurs **for the first time**, not merely what occurs **in the time initially called first**; *restored* means what occurs **again**, not merely what occurs in a later date. This distinction also avoids a proposed infinite regress: if two occurrences were distinguished only by priority and posteriority, and therefore required distinct times, whose own restoration required more times, the argument would proliferate indefinitely. The distinction concerns occurrence-order, not the multiplication of temporal substances.

**Third demonstration:** If it were possible to restore a nonexistent thing with its full quiddity and every individuating accident, it would equally be possible to create **from the outset** a second thing matching it in all those respects, since similar possibilities share a ruling. Yet such a thing could not be distinguished from the returned one, which is impossible. **Reply:** The impossibility of differentiating them **in reality** does not follow; were they genuinely undifferentiated, they would not be two things. Nor is it impossible that the human mind might confuse distinct individuals. Further, the argument would equally prohibit the first creation of two individuals perfectly alike in the proposed respects: the difficulty therefore lies in the theory of individuation and not specifically in re-creation of a nonexistent.

**Fourth demonstration:** A wholly nonexistent subject has no remaining external establishment, cannot be pointed to, and so cannot be judged capable of returning, since predication requires the subject to have some differentiation and establishment. **Reply:** For the Muʿtazilites who hold that nonexistent things preserve their essence or establishment, the answer is immediate. For the author and his colleagues, **mental differentiation and establishment** suffice for predication; external actuality is required only if one asserts that the predicate is already realized as an external property. It is objected that such a proposition would be merely mental, rather than a true proposition about external reality, and so would show at most a return **in thought**. The answer distinguishes the force of the proposition from the mode of considering its subject. In general form it says: whatever meets the subject's description, even as “nonexistent in external reality,” can acquire **existence in external reality**. Even when the proposition is classed as mental, its predicate may be the possibility of real, external existence for the conceived nonexistent. In this respect it resembles “a possible nonexistent can exist” or “a child not yet born may learn.”

**Concluding deflationary reply:** All the demonstrations may be answered by using “re-creation” to mean that there comes to be a being corresponding to the original **in every constituent and characteristic**, so that everyone who sees it judges it to be that very thing. Similarly, “Repeat your words” calls for the same letters, configuration and arrangement. The difference between being earlier or later and called “originated” or “restored” does not matter to this practical definition. One need not settle whether what returns is metaphysically *the identical original* or *a perfect counterpart* in order to establish the truth of bodily resurrection; this much suffices, and none of the preceding objections invalidates it.

**Analytical caution:** The conclusion deliberately weakens what initially seemed a strict numerical-identity thesis; do not collapse the first arguments for *iʿādat al-maʿdūm bi-ʿaynihi* into the final sufficiency claim about reconstitution or perfect similarity.

title: Three theories of resurrection, and the persistence of personal identity
en:
**Investigation two.** The materialist natural philosophers whose opinions are not authoritative either in this question or in philosophy, according to the commentator, deny any resurrection of humanity. They identify a human being with the visible bodily structure, its temperament, faculties and accidents, all of which perish when life ends; nothing remains except dispersed elemental matter, and they reject the return of the nonexistent. This denies reason according to the more accomplished philosophers and revelation according to the more accomplished religious scholars. Galen is reported as suspending judgement because of uncertainty whether the soul is bodily temperament, and so dies with the body, or a substance enduring after death and capable of a return.

Accomplished philosophers and adherents of religion agree on the **reality** of resurrection but disagree over its form. The majority of Muslim theologians maintain that it is **bodily alone**, because for them the spirit is a body spreading through the human organism as fire through coal or water through a rose. The philosophers maintain that it is **spiritual alone**, since the body's form and accidents cease, while the soul is a separate substance not subject to annihilation; its return is to the world of the immaterial by severing bodily attachments. Many Muslim scholars—among them al-Ghazālī, al-Kaʿbī, al-Ḥalīmī, al-Rāghib and the judge Abū Zayd al-Dabūsī—maintain **both spiritual and bodily resurrection**: the immaterial soul is reunited with a body. The commentator notes the popularity of this view among many Sufis, Shīʿites, Karrāmiyya and Christians, as well as among proponents of transmigration.

Al-Rāzī warns against treating the theory of a separately subsisting soul as unbelief merely because transmigrationists and Christians also say souls are separate. Muslims who hold this doctrine believe the souls were **created** and return to bodies in the next world. Transmigrationists, as he represents them, believe souls are eternal and move through bodies in the present world while denying the Resurrection, Paradise and Hell. Christians' unbelief is not attributed to the existence of separate souls but to their doctrine of the Trinity. To affirm an immaterial soul does not undermine any necessary foundation of the faith; it may even strengthen the case for resurrection against certain objections. The commentator cites al-Rāzī's *Nihāyat al-ʿuqūl* in this connection.

Al-Ghazālī wrote extensively on spiritual resurrection, the joys and sufferings of the soul, and their various kinds. This led some people wrongly to accuse him of rejecting bodily resurrection. The accusation is contradicted by explicit affirmations of bodily resurrection in the *Iḥyāʾ* and elsewhere, together with his judgement that its denial is unbelief. His relatively brief explanations of the bodily return reflect his view that it is clear enough without lengthy elaboration.

The language of some who affirm both returns may imply that God forms **a new body from the scattered constituents of the former one**, and reunites with it the soul that persisted after the former body's dissolution. Numerical identity of the two bodies need not be maintained, nor must a thing wholly nonexistent be restored as itself. Scriptural descriptions of the people of Paradise as hairless and beardless, or of the disbeliever's molar being as large as Mount Uḥud, support this interpretation, as does “Whenever their skins have been cooked, We replace them with other skins.” The verse “Is not He who created the heavens and earth capable of creating their likeness?” may be read similarly.

**Objection:** On that view, the one undergoing bodily reward or punishment would not be the one who formerly obeyed or disobeyed. **Reply:** What matters is the **subject of experience** (*idrāk*), which belongs to the soul, even if mediated by bodily organs. The same soul survives, as may the bodily parts that are original and constitutive. We call the person of old age the **same individual** as the child, despite extensive changes in bodily form, appearance, organs and instruments. We do not claim that punishment in old age for a crime in youth punishes a different person.

title: Bodily resurrection and the case against purely figurative interpretation
en:
**The principal evidence for bodily resurrection is transmitted revelation (*samʿ*).** Among religions, Islam makes the doctrine especially explicit; among books, the Qurʾān; and among prophets, Muḥammad. The Muʿtazilites claim to establish bodily resurrection—or even its obligation—by reason. Their reasoning is that God must reward the obedient, punish the disobedient and compensate the deserving; this cannot occur unless the very individuals are restored. Since whatever is indispensable to an obligatory action is itself obligatory, their restoration is necessary. The same argument is invoked for the necessity of restoring persons after annihilation.

This depends, the author says, on the erroneous thesis that **there are obligations binding upon God**, and that refraining from retribution is an injustice that cannot come from Him. Independently, one can question whether physical reconstitution is indispensable and whether spiritual resurrection might suffice. The Muʿtazilite reply identifies the responsible agent with the body or its original constituents rather than the soul alone, so that the proper recipient cannot be rewarded without restoration of bodily parts. **Response:** If one considers the matter by intrinsic reality, the soul is the recipient because obedience and disobedience depend on cognition, volition, actions and movements, all deriving from it. If one considers outward reality, the argument would require restoring every bodily constituent present from the first moment of accountability until death, which the opponents themselves do not hold. Hence it is preferable to rely on transmitted proof.

**Form of the transmitted argument:** Bodily resurrection is possible, and truthful revelation announces it, so it will occur. Possibility follows because the discussion concerns what once existed before ceasing to exist, what was gathered before being dispersed, or what was alive before death. The relevant thing is apt for these states, and its agent is God, whose power extends to all possibilities and whose knowledge comprehends universals and particulars. As for testimony, prophets, especially Muḥammad, have widely and repeatedly proclaimed resurrection. The Qurʾān contains many verses whose bodily meaning is extraordinarily difficult to eliminate through interpretation: “Who will give life to bones when they are decayed? Say: He who first originated them”; emergence from graves toward the Lord; “Who will restore us? Say: He who first fashioned you”; “Does the human being suppose We cannot gather his bones? Indeed, We can restore even his fingertips”; skins speaking to testify against their owners; replacement of burned skins; the splitting of the earth as people rise; and the casting forth of what graves hold. The reports are likewise numerous. Bodily resurrection is therefore a necessity of religion, and its denial, the author maintains, constitutes unbelief.

**Philosophical objection:** Scriptural verses suggesting bodily resurrection are no more numerous or plain than those seemingly implying anthropomorphism, necessitarian determination and other doctrines whose literal senses have been rejected and interpreted figuratively. Why not interpret resurrection texts as representations of the soul's intellectual happiness or misery after bodily separation? Prophets are sent to all people to direct them to truth, perfect their theoretical and practical capacities, and maintain the social order that serves everyone's good. They encourage through promise and deter through threat, using representations of pleasure, pain, perfection and deficiency that the audience understands. Since most people know only sensible pleasure and bodily misery and cannot apprehend the realities of spiritual perfection and intellectual felicity, prophets must address them with **images** of the true resurrection. This is connected to the account attributed to al-Fārābī that religious speech is analogous to philosophical truths through symbols and imaginings.

**Reply:** A nonliteral interpretation becomes necessary only when the literal sense is impossible; here bodily resurrection is not impossible, particularly if the resurrected body may be a perfectly corresponding body rather than numerically the original substance. To reduce the prophets' words and scriptural declarations to merely **fictitious representations** devised for the public interest would attribute lying to the prophets in what they communicate, deliberate misguidance of most humanity, and a lifetime spent promoting falsehood while concealing truth. The audience would naturally understand the outward descriptions as real, whereas the proposed interpretation treats those descriptions as unreal. It would be quite different—and entirely acceptable, in the author's view—to hold that the scriptural descriptions are **both literally true and themselves images or symbols of spiritual reward and pain**. The outward realities are affirmed rather than denied; they may additionally signify intellectual and spiritual realities. Several accomplished Muslim scholars take this view, and he sees no valid objection to it.

title: The objections from bodily annihilation and from intermingled matter
en:
Those denying bodily resurrection offer several objections.

**First:** Bodily resurrection depends on re-creating something wholly nonexistent, which has been shown impossible. If the process is existence after annihilation, this dependence is evident. Even if it means collecting parts after dispersion and reviving them after death, the former composition (*taʾlīf*), temperament (*mizāj*), life and numerous accidents and configurations have ceased to exist, so must be restored. **Reply:** The impossibility of restoring a nonexistent has already been contested. Even if conceded, the doctrine may mean restoring parts to their previous **composition, life and condition**; it need not require that the composite be numerically the original rather than perfectly like it.

**Second: The cannibalism/identity objection.** Suppose one human eats another, and the eaten human's parts are assimilated as food into the eater's body. At resurrection, the parts must be in the eater or in the eaten person's body. Either way one of them is not restored in full as the numerically identical body; there is no reason for assigning the matter to one rather than the other, nor can it be part of both. If the eater was an unbeliever and the eaten person a believer, the wrong person's bodily parts would undergo pleasure or pain.

**Reply:** By “restoration” the author means reconstituting the **original parts** present throughout a person's life, rather than every part gained subsequently through nourishment. For the eater and the eaten alike, the fundamental constituents of their original formation return, so the stated difficulty does not follow.

**Renewed objection:** Food derived from one person's **original** parts could become seed and then form the **original** parts of a new human, recreating the same problem. **Reply:** The objection turns on whether this actually occurs, not whether it is abstractly imaginable. God may preserve those parts from incorporation into another body, all the more from becoming its fundamental constituents. Muʿtazilites claim that divine wisdom obliges Him to preserve them so that the proper person receives recompense; the author's school does not impose such an obligation. He adds that God may preserve the original bodily components even from dispersal so that no recombination is required and the only necessary restoration is of life, form and configuration.

title: Divine purposes, spiritual resurrection and the soul's reunion
en:
**Third objection to bodily resurrection:** If there is no purpose for restoration it would be futile, unworthy of a wise agent. If the purpose returns to God, it would imply a deficiency from which He must be free. If the purpose concerns creatures it must be to convey pain or pleasure. Pain would not be worthy of divine wisdom; pleasure, it is claimed, does not truly exist independently, especially among sensible things, because everything imagined pleasant is mere relief from pain. But the nonexistent and dead are not in pain, and therefore gain no such pleasure from being restored. God would first have to make them suffer and then relieve them—a purposeless production of pain followed by relief.

**Reply:** The author denies that every act of God requires a purpose of that kind, or that lack of such a purpose makes divine action reprehensible. Even conceding purposes, they need not be exhausted by the delivery of pleasure and pain; one might speak of the bestowal of deserved recompense itself. Nor is pleasure merely cessation of pain: pleasure and pain are immediately experienced realities (*wijdāniyyāt*) whose actuality a rational observer does not doubt, as discussed earlier. Finally, the pleasures of the next world need not be identical in intrinsic kind to earthly pleasures, so that the proposed reduction to mere relief from pain would not apply.

**Note on the spiritual return.** Those who accept spiritual resurrection alone, or spiritual **and** bodily resurrection, are the people who hold that rational souls are immaterial substances enduring after the body's dissolution, as supported by earlier arguments and, they maintain, by verses and reports. The former have no further need to prove that a spiritual return exists: by their principles it is the soul's recovery of freedom from bodily bonds or its purification from their darkness, enduring in joy through perfection or pain through deficiency. The latter, having established bodily resurrection, need not separately prove the reunion of each body with **its proper soul**. It would be implausible in reason, and is not transmitted as doctrine, that God restore the body to life under some **other** soul while its own soul remains without function or belongs to another body. The original soul is specially fitted and accustomed to its body's temperament and separated only because the body could no longer receive its government. When that capacity is restored, its connection returns.

The verses “No soul knows what delight of eyes has been hidden for them,” “For those who do good is the best and an increase,” and “God's pleasure is greater” may be taken as allusions to spiritual bliss. Reports concerning the souls of believers, especially the truthful, martyrs and righteous, describe them as residing in the **crops of green birds**, in lamps of light beneath the Throne. Their outward wording can also suggest that spirits are themselves subtle bodies. Thus Imām al-Ḥaramayn, in the *Irshād*, holds that the preferable view is that spirits are subtle bodies interpenetrating visible bodies; God customarily sustains the life of the visible body so long as the spirit remains intermingled with it, and death follows its separation. In reports, a soul is raised and carried in green birds toward Paradise or lowered toward *Sijjīn* in the case of unbelievers. Life, on this account, is an accident by which a substance lives, and the spirit itself also lives through the accident of life if life inheres in it. These are the terms in which Imām al-Ḥaramayn explains his view of spirit.

title: Rival accounts of annihilation (*fanāʾ*)
en:
**Investigation three.** The earlier discussion of bodies noted disagreement about their persistence. Al-Naẓẓām is reported as saying that bodies persist without decomposing; the philosophers, al-Jāḥiẓ and certain Karrāmiyya accept the possibility of their annihilation, though their accounts of eternity differ: philosophers declare bodies beginningless and endless; al-Jāḥiẓ and the Karrāmiyya in question regard them as everlasting but not beginningless. Followers of Abū al-Ḥusayn suspend judgement as to whether annihilation is possible. Among those allowing it, there are three accounts of its cause: a direct act of an annihilating agent; the origination of an incompatible opposite; or the withdrawal of a necessary condition of persistence.

**First account — direct annihilation.** Al-Qāḍī and some Muʿtazilites maintain that God can eliminate the world without an intermediary, making it nonexistent just as He originated it without an intermediary. Abū al-Hudhayl instead says that God commands it, “Perish!” (*ifna*), and it perishes, corresponding to the creative “Be!” (*kun*).

**Second — an opposite of existence or persistence.** Most Muʿtazilites, as represented here, say that a substance perishes through the origination of a contrary accident called *fanāʾ*. They then disagree about its locus and number. Ibn al-Ikhshīd posits an annihilating reality that, although not spatially extended, exists in a definite direction; God's producing it there annihilates all substances. Ibn Shabīb holds that God originates an annihilation in each substance and that it necessitates the nonexistence of that substance in the next instant. Abū ʿAlī and his followers posit one annihilation for every substance, each generated **without a substratum**, resulting in the removal of those substances. Abū Hāshim and his adherents posit one annihilation existing without a substratum that brings about the annihilation of all substances.

**Third — withdrawal of a condition.** Bishr holds that the condition for a substance to persist is *baqāʾ*, an enduringness created by God without a substratum; failing its creation, the substance ceases. Most of the author's colleagues and al-Kaʿbī hold instead that *baqāʾ* inheres in the substance and is created anew at every instant; if God does not create it in the substance, the substance ceases. Imām al-Ḥaramayn identifies the condition with those accidents that a body must possess; if they are not produced in it, the body perishes. According to one reported view of al-Qāḍī, the necessary conditions are its spatial states (*akwān*) created instant by instant; when God ceases creating them, it ceases. Al-Naẓẓām's view is that a body does not persist at all but is originated afresh moment by moment, perishing if God stops creating it.

The author judges most of these theories invalid, especially a theory positing annihilation as an independently existent reality and an **opposite of continued being**, whether subsisting by itself or in a substance, or a separately existent “persistence” having no substratum. He considers their shortcomings sufficiently manifest to require little elaboration.

title: Must bodies cease to exist before resurrection? Suspension of judgement
en:
**Investigation four.** Those accepting both the possibility of annihilation and the resurrection of bodies disagree whether the latter involves **bringing into existence after total extinction** or **collecting parts after separation**. The soundest position, the author states, is **suspension of judgement** (*tawaqquf*), chosen by Imām al-Ḥaramayn. Reason allows substances to cease and then return, or to persist while their familiar accidents cease and their former organization is later restored. No decisive transmitted proof specifies one alternative. God may transform human bodies into the condition of earthy bodies and reassemble them into their former pattern; neither should one rule out that He might annihilate some part and then restore it. God knows best.

Those favouring annihilation before re-creation give several arguments.

**First, alleged prior consensus.** They claim that all agreed before certain late Muʿtazilite and Sunnī dissenters appeared. **Reply:** Such consensus is denied; the Baghdad Muʿtazila collectively opposed it. The Companions did affirm that the Real remains and creation perishes, but “perishing” then meant the loss of things, the death of living beings and separation of body-parts—not a technical claim that the very **substances** composing the world become wholly nonexistent. There is no reason to suppose the Companions debated these fine metaphysical distinctions.

**Second, “He is the First and the Last.”** If “the Last” means last in existence, that seems possible only if everything besides God is entirely nonexistent. This extinction cannot follow the Resurrection, since its consequences endure forever, and must therefore precede it. **Reply:** The verse may mean that God is the source of every existent and the ultimate end of every purpose, or that He alone possesses divinity and the perfections implied by these names. Just as one might say “He was the first and last visitor” meaning he was the **only** visitor, God may be “First and Last” in a non-temporal sense. He may also be last relative to every living creature because He persists beyond its death; or be first as creator and last as provider, as in “He created you, then provided for you.” It cannot mean “last of all things in temporal succession,” since both sides accept that Paradise and its inhabitants are everlasting.

**Third, “Everything perishes except His face.”** Perishing seems to mean real nonexistence, not merely ceasing to be useful, since even dispersed material still points to its Maker and thus has an important use. **Reply:** It can mean that everything is, considered in itself, perishing or contingent, having no claim to existence apart from its cause. Or it may mean death; or cessation of the **particular benefit** appropriate to each thing, as food is said to have perished when it is no longer fit for eating even though it may serve some different purpose. Indicating the Creator is not necessarily the specific intended use of **every** single substance, any more than every word a human writes is written for the explicit purpose of pointing to its author. There is also the idiom “when a man perishes,” meaning dies; or the interpretation that every deed lacking orientation to God's face is destroyed in the sense that no divine reward attaches to it.

**Fourth, “He originates creation, then restores it,” “As We began the first creation We shall restore it,” and “As He began you, so shall you return.”** Since initial creation was from nothing, restoration must be preceded by nothingness; furthermore, a subsequent creation cannot be a genuine restoration without an intervening nonexistence. **Reply:** “Originating creation” need not here mean bringing a thing out of nonbeing; it can mean gathering and arranging, as suggested by “He began human creation from clay.” Thus the beginning of creation can be **seen and investigated**, as in the exhortations to look at how God begins creation. The stronger assertion that *khalq* means **only** composition because verses speak of creating from dust or constructing a falsehood, and therefore does not mean origination, is weak: the lexicographers agree that creating entails producing something through determining it, whether from material or without pre-existing material.

**Fifth, “Everyone upon it is passing away.”** “Passing away” (*fanāʾ*) is allegedly complete nonexistence. **Reply:** It may mean losing a condition that made a thing useful, as in the exhaustion of food and provisions, and can mean the death of every living being on earth. Al-Rāzī observes that if either this verse or “Everything perishes” were taken to assert that **all** things are nonexistent **now**, reinterpretation would already be required. To interpret their participles as “destined to cease” is no more evidently required than “susceptible of cessation.” The commentator connects this to a grammatical dispute about whether active participles can be used literally of future occurrences or require figurative extension; in either case the texts do not conclusively prove universal cessation of all substances.

Those denying complete annihilation and preferring **reassembly after dispersal** also offer arguments.

**First, identity and desert.** If bodies are annihilated, the one who receives reward or punishment will not be the one who deserved it. The consequent is rejected on revealed grounds by the author's school, citing God's not wasting the deeds of the good, and on rational grounds by Muʿtazilites, given their requirement that God reward obedience and punish wrongdoing. The initial inference assumes that whatever is wholly re-created is only a *like*, not the same person. **Reply:** Numerical identity after nonexistence has not been shown impossible. Even if it were, the objection would not touch a theory that preserves **the soul and primary bodily parts** while removing and re-creating other constituents. The primary bearer of moral desert is the enduring soul.

The identity argument is sometimes recast epistemically: after total extinction, how would one know that the raised person was **the original** rather than a new copy? Even when the soul and primary parts persist, former arrangements and distinguishing features may be gone; the problem seems especially acute if the soul is itself regarded as a body. **Reply:** What revealed evidence gives is God's delivery of recompense to those who deserve it, not necessarily our ability to identify every resurrected individual **by inspection**. God knows, and He may create immediate knowledge or furnish a manifest particular or general means of recognition. Preserving the primary parts may also provide sufficient continuity; the argument at most defeats a theory of complete destruction of every constituent.

**Second, purposeless annihilation.** Muʿtazilites argue that the wise agent must pursue a purpose and cannot act idly. Annihilation benefits nobody, for benefits presuppose existence and ordinarily life; neither is it itself a recompense, an interrogation, a reckoning or a punishment. **Reply:** Purposes are not exhausted by benefits or immediate recompense. God may have wisdoms unknown to creatures; warning of annihilation may encourage responsibility, display divine greatness and independence, and manifest His unique endurance, and the actual annihilation would make the announcement true.

The identity and purposelessness objections can also be directed against the **dispersal** theory: loss of configurations may remove the features by which individuals differ, while dispersal seems to benefit no one. **Reply:** Some distinctive features need not vanish, such as a substance's relation to certain directions; even if they do, the enduring original constituents—not an immutable set of accidents and determinations—are the bearers of identity and desert. Someone harmed another person while young, robust and physically whole can later be punished when old, emaciated and missing members without becoming a different person. Dispersal can also serve the purposes of teaching through signs and of enabling pleasure and suffering through the arrangement of recompense.

**Third, scriptural descriptions.** Accounts of Abraham's question “Lord, show me how You give life to the dead,” the man passing a ruined town, the re-clothing of bones with flesh, and verses likening rising again to observable regeneration, point to **reviving what has died and gathering what has been scattered**, not creating ex nihilo after every substance has vanished. Verses describing human beings scattered like moths and mountains like carded wool similarly suggest separation rather than complete extinction. **Reply:** Such texts do not **exclude** an interval of total nonexistence merely because they do not establish one. They were addressed to questions about revival and gathering because those processes are easier to visualize and observe. They must also be weighed against the texts invoked by the opposing side. Therefore the author's preferred **suspension of judgement** remains appropriate.

title: Whether Paradise and Hell already exist
en:
**Investigation five.** The majority of Muslims affirm that Paradise and Hell have **already been created**, against Abū Hāshim, al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār and like-minded Muʿtazilites, who hold that they are created only at the time of recompense. Two principal proofs are offered.

**First:** The account of Adam and Eve entering Paradise, being expelled after eating from the tree, and sewing leaves of Paradise to cover themselves, as described in scripture and acknowledged by consensus before the appearance of the opponents. To identify this place as an ordinary garden in the earthly world is, the author argues, to treat religious discourse frivolously and defy the established community's reading. And nobody, he says, adopts the view that Paradise was created but Hell was not; establishing the one therefore establishes the other.

**(3) Cosmological impossibility:** If the two abodes now exist, they must be in this world or another. (The argument also invokes a disputed identification of transmigration with souls returning to bodies in the elemental world.) If they exist in a second world, that world's directions must likewise be fixed by centre and circumference, making it spherical. It would touch this world at at most one point and would entail an **empty interval** between the worlds; void is supposed impossible. Determination by centre and circumference concerns *up and down* in particular, not all relational directions. The proof against rupture pertains, even on the philosophers' reasoning, to the outermost sphere; two enclosed worlds could resemble two epicycles within one larger orb without a void. Their elements may differ in nature, and being in one world may not be the natural place of an element belonging to the other. Nor is transmigration merely a soul returning to **its own** body; it is an attachment to **another** body in this world.

**Further objection:** This reasoning would also refute the creation of Paradise and Hell at the Resurrection, as resurrected humans and earthly elements would still have to inhabit a place beyond the unrupturable spheres. **Reply:** If the present cosmos were altogether annihilated and another created containing Paradise, Hell, humans and the relevant elements, there would be no need to breach the presently existing spheres. Hence the argument is specifically directed against simultaneous existence with this cosmos.

Most place Paradise above the seven heavens and beneath the Throne, citing “near it is the Garden of Refuge” and the report “The roof of Paradise is the Throne of the Merciful”; Hell is commonly placed beneath the seven earths. The author prefers to **entrust the exact location to the knowledge of the All-Knowing, All-Aware**, rather than claiming certainty where no decisive text exists.

title: Questioning and punishment in the grave
en:
**Investigation six.** Muslims are said to agree on the reality of questioning by Munkar and Nakīr in the grave, the punishment of unbelievers there, and the punishment of some transgressors. Dissent has been attributed to certain Muʿtazilites, but a later Muʿtazilite writer reports that denial belonged to Ḍirār b. ʿAmr; the Muʿtazila as a group were wrongly associated with it because of his proximity to them. Others then followed this denial.

**Evidence from scripture and transmitted reports.** The people of Pharaoh are “exposed to the fire, morning and evening” before the Day of Resurrection, since the verse distinguishes that exposure from the command on the Day of the Hour to enter the severest punishment. Of Noah's people, “they were drowned and then brought into a fire,” the sequence implied by *fa-* indicating an immediate successor. In “Our Lord, You have made us die twice and given us life twice,” one of the two lives is taken to occur in the grave, where it permits an anticipatory experience of recompense. The martyrs are “alive with their Lord, receiving provision, rejoicing in what God has given them.” The author further cites a body of reports convergent in general import, including “The grave is a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of fire,” the Prophet's passing two graves and declaring their occupants under punishment, and the account of two angels entering the grave with iron clubs and asking about one's Lord, religion and prophet. The Prophet's repeated seeking of refuge from grave-punishment is also invoked.

**Scriptural objections.** The verse “They will taste no death therein except the first death” seems to allow only one death before Paradise; but if grave life occurs, a death must follow it before resurrection, making two. **Reply:** The exception can be *disconnected*, meaning “but they have already tasted the first death”; or a rhetorical, impossible condition stressing the uninterrupted bliss of Paradise, as if one said: “If death could occur there, it would have to be that first death which has already passed”—an impossibility. The expression “first death” need only be relative to an imagined death within Paradise that the verse denies, not a declaration that a second death actually occurs. To treat “first” merely as “the death actually realised as opposed to an imaginary death” is grammatically problematic, given the form expressing singular occurrence.

Other verses say “You were dead, then He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will give you life,” and “You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice.” If grave life were counted, there might be three revivifications: life on earth, in the grave and at resurrection. “You cannot make those in graves hear” appears to deny consciousness to the buried. **Reply:** Mentioning two cases does not logically exclude a third. The sequence of dying and reviving can comprise more than one instance, because a verb need not denote a single occurrence; however, the author admits that the second *thumma* (“then”) makes that construction somewhat strained. More plausibly, the verse focuses on earthly death and final resurrection, omitting the grave's lesser and less apparent life because it is not suited to the passage's argument for divine power and the necessity of belief. In the confession of the condemned, two deaths and revivifications can instead refer to episodes in the world and grave, omitting final resurrection because its reality is immediately present to them; or to grave and resurrection on the interpretation that what counts is revived awareness entailing certain knowledge of God and confession of sin. The comparison of unbelievers to the buried in “You cannot make them hear” remains an analogy involving ordinary dead persons; it does not settle what exceptional experience God may create.

**Rational objections.** Pleasure, pain, interrogation and speech require life and cognition, and life allegedly requires an intact bodily structure and temperament. Yet observers see a dead or executed person remain motionless, mute and without any visible trace of pleasure or suffering. A corpse may be placed in an extremely narrow coffin or recess where sitting as described in reports appears impossible; grains scattered on its chest do not move. A body may be devoured, burned to ashes or scattered by the winds. How could all those states coexist with renewed life, suffering, questioning and answering? To allow such invisible events, opponents contend, is sophistry akin to declaring that the dead person's bed is alive and converses while remaining manifestly unchanged.

**General reply:** These objections establish unfamiliarity, not impossibility, just as with other extraordinary acts. If a truthful reporter establishes their occurrence, they are to be accepted. **Detailed reply:** Life need not require an intact organic configuration. Even if it does, some constituents sufficient for such a structure may remain. Punishment and questioning may be borne by the spirit (understood as a subtle body) or enduring fundamental parts, in a manner invisible to the observer, or God may conceal them from human and jinn perception for a wisdom we do not grasp. They may occur even if the body is within an animal. A divine agent who creates life and death can enlarge a grave or coffin, sustain a few grains motionless upon a moving body, and produce other unusual states. The charge of sophistry would be apt only where no proof or truthful report supports such phenomena.

The author nevertheless rejects two reported rival explanations. Some Ṣāliḥiyya and Karrāmiyya are said to permit punishment **without life**, denying that life is necessary for perception; Ibn al-Rāwandī is said to regard every corpse as **alive**, making death a general incapacity for voluntary actions rather than an opposite of life or a negation of knowledge. These do not accord with the author's principles.

**Conclusion:** Adherents of truth agree that God restores to the dead person a **kind of life** sufficient for experiencing pleasure or pain, as supported by scriptural and transmitted testimony. They withhold judgement about whether the soul itself is reunited with the body in the grave. Life without the full spirit is not impossible; the complete life attended by power and voluntary actions requires more than the limited life of the grave. They agree that God does not create normal voluntary power and actions in the corpse, which is why its life is not evident, as with someone in a cataleptic or unresponsive condition. The author acknowledges a difficulty in reconciling this limited life with the reports that the deceased actually answers Munkar and Nakīr.

title: Reckoning, the Bridge, Balance and Basin
en:
**Investigation seven: Other transmitted matters pertaining to resurrection.** These are matters intrinsically possible, asserted by the Book and prophetic reports, and affirmed by the agreement of the community; consequently their affirmation is true and assent to them obligatory.

**The Reckoning (*muḥāsaba*).** The Qurʾān says “God is swift in reckoning,” and the author cites the counsel “Call yourselves to account before you are called to account.” Its terrors include standing before God—variously reckoned as one thousand years, fifty thousand years, less or more, the author declining to fix a duration—“Stop them, for they are to be questioned,” and the ranks of spirits and angels standing without speech save by divine permission. Records will be distributed and received, sometimes in the right hand, the Qurʾān promising an easy reckoning; each soul encounters an opened record of its deeds. There will be interrogation and the testimony of ten classes of witnesses: tongues, hands, feet, hearing, eyes, skins, earth, night, day and the noble guardian angels. Scriptural verses describe bodily members testifying; a transmitted saying represents each new night and day as testifying to what humans do within it. Every soul comes with a driver and witness. Faces change in colour—some bright, laughing and hopeful, others darkened or covered in gloom—and the blessed and condemned are proclaimed as such. The author cites a report of angels standing near the two pans of the Balance and announcing irreversible happiness or wretchedness according to which pan prevails.

Why reckon and display these terrors when God already knows everything? To exhibit publicly the ranks of the perfected and the disgrace of the deficient, magnifying the former's delights and joy and the latter's shame and suffering; and to encourage good acts and deter evil acts in advance. Whether prophets, saints, righteous and reverent people experience these terrors is uncertain, but the author considers their preservation from them more apparent in light of the angels' promise “Do not fear and do not grieve” and “The friends of God shall have no fear, nor shall they sorrow.”

**The Bridge (*al-ṣirāṭ*).** A bridge stretches above Hell, reached by all the earlier and later peoples. It is described in reports as finer than a hair and sharper than a sword, and its crossing may be the “coming to” the fire of which the Qurʾān says “Not one of you but will come to it.” Al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār and numerous Muʿtazilites deny such a bridge as impossible to traverse, or else as an undeserved torment to believers and the righteous. They instead take it to be a road to Paradise or Hell, the clear proofs of truth, religious observances such as prayer and almsgiving, or the bad deeds over which one must pass in judgement. **Reply:** Traversing a bridge of this sort is possible for the omnipotent Creator, no less than walking on water or flying in air, although it departs from common experience. God renders the crossing easy for whom He wishes: reports describe some passing like lightning, others like wind or horses, others struggling as their legs fail and hands cling, and others falling facedown.

**The Balance (*al-mīzān*).** Scripture says “We shall set up just balances on the Day of Resurrection” and contrasts heavy and light balances. Many exegetes take the Balance as a real instrument with two pans, a tongue and supports, because its ordinary meaning is possible, and reports describe it thus. Some Muʿtazilites object that deeds are accidents, and vanished accidents cannot be weighed, interpreting the verse instead as justice measured in everything. The plural “balances,” they say, fits justice better than one literal instrument. Some propose that “balance” signifies the power of discerning: sight measures colours, hearing sounds, taste flavours, each other sense its objects, and knowledge or intellect the intelligibles. **Reply:** One may weigh the **records of deeds**, or deeds may be made luminous bodies and bad deeds dark bodies. The plural could magnify the solemnity of the event, or each responsible person might have a balance while there remains one great Balance manifesting the majesty of the occasion.

**The Basin (*al-ḥawḍ*).** The Qurʾān's “We have given you al-Kawthar” and reports of the Prophet's Basin are invoked. One report describes a basin a month's journey across, equal at its corners, with water whiter than milk, fragrance sweeter than musk, and drinking vessels more numerous than the stars; whoever drinks from it will never thirst again. Asked where he should be sought on the Day of Assembly, the Prophet is reported as answering: at the Bridge; if not found there, at the Balance; and if not there, at the Basin. The descriptions and precise attribution of reports remain to be verified separately before publication.

title: Philosophical descriptions of the afterlife
en:
**Investigation eight: The philosophers' account of Paradise, Hell, reward and punishment.** Those who accept a **world of images or exemplars** (*ʿālam al-mithāl*) also affirm Paradise, Hell and the detailed contents of revelation, but locate them in that imaginal order rather than among the purely sensible bodies affirmed by the theologians. Most other philosophers understand the relevant states as **intellectual pleasures and pains**.

On this account the human soul, whether beginningless as Plato was taken to hold or generated as Aristotle was taken to hold, persists for ever after separation from the body. It remains in joy through the intellectual perfections and apprehensions it attained—its felicity, reward and Paradise, varying according to its rank and condition—or it suffers through the absence of perfection and corruption of belief—its misery, punishment and Hell, with their different degrees. During embodied life the soul does not attend fully to these states because it is immersed in bodily governance, the turbid conditions of nature and attachments and hindrances removed by separation at death. Scriptural descriptions of reward, punishment and related matters are accordingly read as **figurative descriptions** of degrees of felicity and suffering, intellectual joys and pains, and movement between the levels of misery and happiness.

For these philosophers, eternal misery belongs to **settled compound ignorance** (*al-jahl al-murakkab al-rāsikh*) and entrenched wickedness opposed to virtuous character, not to simple ignorance or character uncommitted to either great vice or virtue. The misery attached to the latter is transient or perhaps does not occur at all. The lack of intellectual perfection can result from (i) privation, such as an innate deficiency in the rational faculty; or (ii) a positive obstacle opposed to perfection, which may be firmly established or not. Each of these three cases may affect theoretical or practical reason, producing six possibilities.

Deprivation arising from an innate deficiency in either faculty cannot be remedied after death but entails **no punishment** on that account. An entrenched obstacle in theoretical reason, such as compound ignorance that has become an inseparable form of the soul, is likewise incurable, but brings **perpetual suffering**. The remaining classes—unsettled theoretical errors such as those held by ordinary imitators, and firmly or weakly entrenched practical vices or acquired dispositions—may depart after death, either because they lack stability or because they arose through bodily actions and temperaments which themselves have ended. Suffering varies in severity and duration according to the strength of the defect and the speed with which it fades.

This analysis concerns souls aware that perfection is possible, whether they have acquired its opposite, distracted themselves from pursuing it, or neglected intellectual cultivation. Souls that are sound but possess neither intellectual perfection nor its opposite, nor any strong desire for it, may remain within an expanse of divine mercy, free from their bodies and enjoying a felicity suited to them, without the suffering of the wicked.

Some philosophers regard it as impossible for such souls to lack all awareness; they must therefore become related to **other bodies** because they can imagine only through bodily instruments. If they become the substantial principles and governing souls of those bodies, this is **transmigration**. If not, another proposal, attributed to Avicenna and al-Fārābī, is that they attach to celestial bodies without governing them as souls, merely using them as instruments of imagination. They then produce and experience forms corresponding to their previous beliefs and conceptions, and thus encounter afterlife rewards as they imagine them.
